title: Isaac Newton went undercover in taverns to catch counterfeiters for the Royal Mint

cover.alt: Godfrey Kneller's 1689 oil portrait of Isaac Newton, with long grey hair, an open white shirt and a brown gown, against a dark background.

body: In 1696 Isaac Newton became Warden of the Royal Mint, and in 1699 its Master, a job he kept until his death in 1727. He arrived during the Great Recoinage, when counterfeit coins were a serious problem. Newton chased the coiners himself: he made himself a justice of the peace in all the home counties, gathered much of the evidence in person while disguised as a regular in bars and taverns, and between June 1698 and Christmas 1699 cross-examined more than 100 witnesses, informers and suspects. He also made coins more uniform in weight, and saved the Treasury £41,510.

slides.question: During the Great Recoinage of 1696, what share of the coins taken in did Newton estimate were counterfeit?
slides.explanation: About one coin in five, by Newton's estimate.

slides.label: coiners Newton successfully prosecuted
slides.text: Among them was William Chaloner, who was hanged.

slides.heading: Guineas got more consistent under Newton
slides.note: Standard deviation of guinea weights: how far a typical coin strayed from the average.

slides.alt: Both sides of a small gold coin beside a scale bar: the laureate head of King George I, and four shields arranged in a cross.
slides.caption: A gold half guinea of George I, dated 1717: the year Britain capped the guinea's value at 21 silver shillings after a report by Newton.

slides.heading: A gold standard by accident?
slides.text: On 21 September 1717 Newton reported to the Treasury. In December a royal proclamation banned exchanging a gold guinea for more than 21 silver shillings. Silver grew scarce, and Britain shifted in effect from a silver standard to its first gold standard. It is still debated whether Newton meant this to happen.

slides.question: Why was counterfeiting so dangerous for the coiners Newton hunted?
options: It meant exile to the colonies
slides.explanation: Counterfeiting was high treason, punishable by being hanged, drawn and quartered.
